value: spatial resolution estimated at 15 to 40 degrees, depending on the assumed contrast sensitivity
method: behavioural: attraction of walking animals to dark targets of differing angular size (dual bars and piecewise sine gratings), combined with 3D reconstruction, optics and modelling
conditions: adults of 22 to 41 mm body length collected from decomposing logs in Tallaganda State Forest, kept individually at 19 C under 12 h:12 h light:dark; tested in the night phase in an otherwise dark room lit by a 100 W bulb; one of 52 animals was excluded for not responding to bright light, 50 were tested; 343 trials, 21 to 27 per stimulus including 23 controls; the range comes from assuming contrast sensitivity of 5 to 20; animals were tested with stimuli of the same average luminance as the background (abstract)

source.authors: Kirwan JD, Graf J, Smolka J, Mayer G, Henze MJ, Nilsson D-E
source.title: Low resolution vision in a velvet worm (Onychophora)

quote: Depending on the assumed contrast sensitivity of the animals, we estimate the spatial resolution to be in the range 15–40 deg.
note: Filed under behaviour_vision because the paper gives an angle in degrees, not cycles/degree. Same paper's abstract: the animals cannot spot or visually identify prey or conspecifics beyond a few centimetres; a 10 deg dark target was probably detected, a 6.7 deg one not. The conditions text comes from the open PDF on the publisher site read through the fetch tool. Licence shown is the publisher user licence, not a CC licence. Euperipatoides rowelli has a different acuity row on main from a modelling paper (10.1371/journal.pcbi.1008808); this is the behavioural measurement.

value: EOD waveform and the sequence of pulse intervals were both necessary and sufficient for species recognition by males (electric cues alone)
method: behavioural playback of electric organ discharge (EOD) waveforms paired with conspecific, heterospecific or scrambled pulse-interval sequences (five conditions); time near each playback electrode scored from infrared video as strength of preference
conditions: 12 sexually mature males of this species; five playback conditions; Males spent significantly more time near the conspecific EOD waveform in playback conditions I to III and showed no preference in condition IV (scrambled pulse intervals) or V. Two sympatric species tested with the same design.

source.authors: Nagel R, Kirschbaum F, Hofmann V, Engelmann J, Tiedemann R
source.title: Electric pulse characteristics can enable species recognition in African weakly electric fish species

quote: While the EOD waveform and SPI were both necessary and sufficient for species recognition in C. compressirostris males, C. tamandua males apparently utilize other, non-electric modalities.
note: CC BY 4.0 per Crossref. Sample sizes, stimuli and Results from the nature.com page read through the fetch tool; the quote is the abstract sentence as read on ADS. The same sentence supports both species rows; they are two findings (one per species).

value: males apparently use other, non-electric modalities for species recognition (no significant preference for conspecific electric playback in conditions I to IV)
method: behavioural playback of electric organ discharge (EOD) waveforms paired with conspecific, heterospecific or scrambled pulse-interval sequences (five conditions); time near each playback electrode scored from infrared video as strength of preference
conditions: 10 sexually mature males of this species; five playback conditions; In condition V males favoured the heterospecific C. compressirostris signal, only marginally (p = 0.049). Two sympatric species tested with the same design.

value: larvae are repelled by light; repellence rises as wavelength falls, with the maximal response at 400 nm violet light
method: behavioural: choice of larvae between lit and dark sides of an arena under 14 quasi-monochromatic stimuli (368 to 743 nm), repellency rate per wavelength
conditions: 300 freshly collected larvae from the River Ipoly (June and August 2020 and 2021), each tested once in 20 blocks of 15; dark-adapted at least 45 min at 25 +/- 1 C; three intensities (9.48e11, 9.48e12, 9.48e13 photons/cm2/s), repellence rose with intensity at every wavelength; dark controls gave no directed movement; 12 of 14 wavelengths differed from dark controls, and 517 nm and 743 nm gave no significant response; repellence was negligible above 500 nm; per-wavelength values are in figures only

source.authors: Mészáros Á, Kriska G, Egri Á
source.title: Wavelength-specific negatively phototactic responses of the burrowing mayfly larvae Ephoron virgo

quote: We established that the magnitude of repellence increased with decreasing wavelength and the maximal responses were elicited by 400 nm violet light.
note: Read on the Hungarian repository copy (real.mtak.hu); the licence visible there is the Company of Biologists copyright line and Crossref gives the publisher user licence (not CC). The paper attributes the 743 nm null to near-zero compound-eye sensitivity and assumes 517 nm is still repellent. A behaviour finding, not a spectral sensitivity curve.

value: five of the eight species detected 50 to 3600 Hz
method: auditory evoked potentials (AEP) to 50 ms tone bursts at 15 frequencies from 50 to 4000 Hz from an underwater speaker in a soundproof chamber; unanaesthetised fish held in a harness with subdermal needle electrodes
conditions: eight species: Piaractus brachypomus n=10, Metynnis lippincottianus n=10, Myloplus rubripinnis n=3, Myleus schomburgkii n=8, Serrasalmus elongatus n=5, S. spilopleura n=7, Pygocentrus nattereri n=10, P. piraya n=5 (55 to 112 mm standard length); aquaria at 26 +/- 1 C, 12 h light:dark; the species are not named in the sentence, so the row is graded as a family; the paper's Discussion places all eight species' best sensitivity at low frequencies (50 to 900 Hz) and the abstract says only slight threshold differences were found

source.authors: Mélotte G, Parmentier E, Michel C, Herrel A, Boyle K
source.title: Hearing capacities and morphology of the auditory system in Serrasalmidae (Teleostei: Otophysi)

quote: Five species out of eight were able to detect frequencies ranging from 50 to 3600 Hz (Fig. 2).
note: CC BY 4.0 per Crossref. Methods and quote read on the nature.com page through the fetch tool (Table 1 per-species values were not returned). Pygocentrus nattereri was more sensitive than Piaractus brachypomus at 300 Hz and by over 27 dB SPL at 1200 Hz. Species-level hearing ranges need Table 1.
